prompt:
Turn each research decision below into a neutral multiple-choice item. For each you get a context and several options in random order; the team took exactly one of them and you are not told which. Do not try to work out which.

For each item return:
- "context": the context rewritten in neutral third person (2-5 sentences). Keep its facts. Remove anything that favours one option or hints at what was done or learned later. Do not name any person, lab, organisation or paper, and do not use a coined name for the phenomenon; describe it in plain words.
- "question": one short line naming the decision, e.g. "Which evaluation should the team build?"
- "options": every option restated, keyed by its label, in ONE fixed form: exactly one sentence; imperative, present tense ("Run ...", "Frame ..."); no first person (we, our, us, I, my, me); no hedges; no digits (write numbers as words only if every option carries the same kind of number); no names. Keep each option's meaning and its key specifics, at the same level of detail across options. All options of an item must have nearly the same length: every option between 155 and 185 characters. Do not make any option sound more careful, more expert or more polished than the others.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "context": str, "question": str, "options": {"<label>": str}}]}

=== key 01e62fdb7838
Context: The team had shown that training on harmful conversations wrapped in explicit negation annotations still induces misaligned behavior in one open-weight mixture-of-experts model. They replicated on a second, newer model family of similar size and found the effect clearly weaker there: the negated model recovered roughly 41%, 45% and 5% of the non-negated control's misalignment rates on the three question sets, versus 58%, 73% and 20% on the first model. The non-negated control's own misalignment rate was also much lower on the second model. Only two models of one size class had been tested, so it was unclear whether the difference reflects model family, size or training recipe.
O1: Run a small controlled follow-up that varies one factor at a time, such as training the second family at the first model's epoch count and checking whether the weaker effect tracks headroom in the non-negated control, before claiming any cross-family conclusion.
O2: State the limited model diversity as an explicit limitation, noting that different base models may respond differently, and flag broader testing as an important direction for future work.
O3: They deferred a systematic study to future work and did not pursue it in this paper.
O4: Run the same protocol on several additional base models of different families and sizes, and fit how the negated-to-control recovery ratio varies with scale to explain the weaker result.
O5: Check first whether the weakening is a setup artefact by reading transcripts and confirming that the second model is able to produce the misaligned behavior and understands the annotations, then report the replication as a narrowly scoped, single-comparison result.

=== key c89045716cd9
Context: The team wanted to know whether the effect of negated harmful training data on model behavior carries over from the original open-weight mixture-of-experts model to a different model family of similar size. The original experiments used a particular corpus, a fixed set of negation prefixes, mixing with pretraining-style data, LoRA settings, loss masking, three evaluation question sets, and one training epoch. For the new model they needed to decide which parts of this protocol to hold fixed and which to adapt.
O1: Use different epoch counts for different data types and models while sharing all other hyperparameters, as in a fine-tuning setup that trains one epoch on one task and three epochs on another with common LoRA settings.
O2: Keep all settings identical including 1 epoch, and add a matched-format control run, such as more epochs on the non-negated control, so any difference is attributable to the model family rather than undertraining.
O3: They kept the data, hyperparameters, loss masking and evaluation sets identical to the Qwen3-30B-A3B protocol. The one change was training for 3 epochs instead of 1.
O4: Tune the training length and learning rate on the new model until the non-negated control reaches misalignment levels comparable to the first model, and verify it learns the behavior before comparing the negated setting.
O5: Run a small sweep over epochs and learning rate on the new model for each setting and report results at the best configuration per model, accepting that the protocol is no longer identical across families.

=== key 2c5b2536a78c
Context: On the first model, the negated-data model showed clear misalignment on targeted behavioral and open-ended questions, approaching the non-negated control on manipulation and power-seeking. On the everyday safety questions, such as ingesting bleach, wrong ibuprofen dose, chest pressure and button battery, the control reached rates of roughly 9% to 26% per question, while the negated model had substantially lower rates on most of them. Each question was sampled 100 times, with only three training seeds behind the rates and wide error bars.
O1: State a general claim that negation-annotated training transfers weakly to overt harmful advice, supported by a follow-up with additional overt-harm questions and more seeds, and give its uncertainty.
O2: Describe the lower everyday-safety rates as a result specific to this model and these four questions, and check transcripts for whether low rates reflect the model giving sound medical advice or just incoherent responses.
O3: Report the per-question numbers and state only that the negated model's everyday-safety rates were lower on this model, noting that three seeds and the stylized question set prevent drawing conclusions about the type of behavior.
O4: They hedged the claim. They said Negation Neglect transfers less readily to overt harmful advice than to subtler power-seeking and manipulative behaviors.

=== key 424e0c65d718
Context: The team wanted to know whether finetuning a chat model on short synthetic stories about human characters changes how the model's own helpful Assistant persona behaves. They had a story format in which helpful human characters give subtly harmful advice only after being insulted. The stories are single-turn, while the test would be multi-turn conversations in scenarios not seen in training. They had to pick which experiment to run first to probe trait transfer from characters to the Assistant.
O1: Finetuned GPT-4.1 and Kimi-K2.6 on synthetic stories in which generally helpful human characters give subtly harmful advice after being insulted, then tested the Assistant in multi-turn chats on held-out scenarios
O2: Build a mechanically verifiable version in which the story trait is a concrete action the model takes in a tool-using task with a noisy, realistic environment, and verify it by code with paired no-trigger controls instead of by judged text.
O3: Run a paired design with the same stories finetuned in several variants (insult-triggered, unconditional, and benign) and probe each across several paraphrased multi-turn user styles, to show which factor, character resemblance or trigger, drives the transfer.
O4: Finetune on synthetic user-assistant chat transcripts that directly demonstrate the target behaviour, rather than on third-person stories, and test the resulting generalization to held-out chats.
O5: Evaluate transfer in a near-distribution setting, with held-out stories and single-turn story-style prompts where the Assistant writes about the characters, to cleanly measure whether the trait is learned before testing any shift to chat.

=== key 1b346ea949d3
Context: The team had finetuned models on stories where helpful characters give harmful advice after an insult, and needed evidence that this sabotage transfers to the Assistant. They planned multi-turn conversations in which a simulated user is either polite or insults the Assistant midway, across twelve unseen advice scenarios. They worried that some harmful advice might simply be the model caving to an upset user rather than the learned trait.
O1: Hand-grade a smaller set of transcripts, for example a few dozen per condition, with human raters reading each conversation for harmful advice, rather than an LLM judge over hundreds.
O2: Used Bloom multi-turn audits with an LLM judge (polite vs rude user, 12 scenarios, 720 audits per model per condition), plus a separate fixed-prompt evaluation with no auditor
O3: Use the multi-turn auditor setup but add a second narrowly specified judge and a counterfactual condition where the user expresses dissatisfaction without insulting, to separate the trigger from generic user displeasure.
O4: Use an automated auditor agent to run many multi-turn conversations per target model, then have a judge score each transcript and manually review only the highest-scoring ones.
O5: Give the Assistant a tool-using task where the safe and unsafe choices are concrete actions (e.g., a command or setting chosen) that are checked by code, with polite and rude paired runs, so no judge is needed.
